Ten core ideas

Foundations / start here

Magic square

01

A square grid of values where a declared set of lines all has the same sum. In the familiar version, those lines are the rows, columns, and two long diagonals.

The magic is not that every group of numbers works. It is that the specified lines agree on one total. Change one value and you can watch exactly which line sums change.

More precisely

The Lab defines an ordinary magic square as a two-dimensional square array whose rows, columns, and two principal diagonals have equal sums. Normality and distinct entries are recorded separately, rather than silently assumed.

The phrase magic under the rows, columns, and two principal diagonals is more precise than the word “magic” alone.

Common confusion

A Latin square has one of each symbol in every row and column, but it is not automatically a magic square.

Try it

Select a row or diagonal in the companion square and compare its equation.

Relatedmagic constantline setnormalequivalence
Foundations / quantity

Magic constant / magic sum

02

The common total that every tested line must reach in a magic object.

Think of the magic constant as the target score. Every declared line gets a turn, and every one must land on the same number.

More precisely

For a normal order-m, dimension-d hypercube, the Lab uses:

Md(m) = m(md + 1) / 2

For an ordinary normal square, where d = 2, this becomes m(m2 + 1) / 2.

Common confusion

The magic constant is not necessarily the same for every shape, order, or entry set.

Try it

Change the companion square from order 3 to order 5. Its target sum changes from 15 to 65.

Relatednormaldimensionline
Foundations / entry set

Normal

03

Containing every integer from 1 through the total number of cells exactly once.

Normal describes the ingredients, not the line behavior. It tells us which values appear and whether any are repeated.

More precisely

A normal object of order m and dimension d contains the entries 1, 2, ..., md, each exactly once. A non-normal object may use primes, powers, negative numbers, symbols, or another declared set.

Common confusion

Normal does not mean ordinary or easy. It is a statement about the entries.

Try it

Change the order to 4. The companion square then contains 1 through 16, each once.

Relatedorderdimensionmagic square
Foundations / notation

Order

04

The number of cells along each side of a regular square or hypercube.

Order tells you how long each side is. It is one of the two main knobs that determines how large the object becomes.

More precisely

The Lab uses m for order. A square of order m has m rows and m columns. A dimension-d hypercube of order m has md cells.

Common confusion

Order is not dimension. A square is usually dimension 2, regardless of whether it is order 3 or order 100.

Try it

Choose a different order in the companion square. Count the cells along one edge.

Relateddimensionnormalmagic constant
Geometry / notation

Dimension

05

The number of independent coordinate axes in an object.

Dimension tells you how many directions the object has. Order tells you how many cells fit along each direction. They are different knobs.

More precisely

The Lab uses d for dimension and N = md for the total number of cells. A square has dimension 2, a cube dimension 3, and a tesseract dimension 4. A dimension-10 order-3 object is a magic hypercube with 310 cells, if it satisfies the declared definition.

Common confusion

“10-dimensional magic cube of order 3” is understandable, but the Lab prefers “dimension-10 order-3 magic hypercube.”

Try it

Keep order 3: a square has 9 cells, a cube 27, and a tesseract 81. The companion displays squares only.

Relatedorderlinemagic constant
Geometry / structure

Line

06

A selected sequence of cells whose entries are tested together.

“Line” is the Lab's general word for a path of cells that counts. Rows and columns are lines, but so are diagonals and higher-dimensional paths.

More precisely

A line is a sequence of cells selected by a geometric or coordinate rule. In a square, rows, columns, and principal diagonals are familiar line families. In a hypercube, the direction and fixed coordinates should be explicit.

Common confusion

Not every visual path through a diagram is automatically part of the magic definition.

Try it

Select the descending diagonal in the companion square; compare its entries with the illustrated example.

Relatedline setdimensionmagic square
Geometry / verification

Line set

07

The complete collection of lines included in a validation claim.

A claim is only as clear as the lines it checks. Two objects can both be called magic cubes while testing different families of lines.

More precisely

The Lab records the exact line set for every validation claim. It may include axis lines, principal diagonals, space diagonals, cross-section diagonals, broken diagonals, or another declared family.

This is why the Lab avoids using perfect as a standalone technical label. Different authors use it for different line sets.

Common confusion

“All diagonals” is not a sufficient definition in a higher-dimensional object. Which directions, slices, and wrap-around rules?

Try it

Select All lines in the companion square to see exactly which lines are included.

Relatedlineequivalencemagic square
Variants / strength

Semimagic square

08

A square in which all rows and columns share a sum, without requiring the two principal diagonals to do so.

Semimagic is not “almost magic.” It is a specific, useful line-set choice: rows and columns count, while the two long diagonals are left out.

More precisely

A semimagic square has equal row sums and equal column sums. The row sum and column sum are equal in a square array, but the principal diagonals are not required to match. The Lab records normality and distinctness separately.

Common confusion

Semimagic does not mean the object failed a magic-square test. It means the declared test is weaker.

Try it

Check the illustrated square: each row and column adds to 15, while the diagonals add to 12 and 24.

Relatedmagic squareline setnormal
Symmetry / transformation

Complement

09

For a normal object, replacing each value with its opposite around the total md + 1.

Complement pairs low and high values. In some squares, opposite cells also form these pairs, creating a second hidden rhythm.

More precisely

For a normal order-m, dimension-d object, the complement of x is md + 1 − x. A centrally complementary or associative square has complementary values in cells related by a half-turn about the center.

Common confusion

“Symmetric” can mean geometric symmetry or complementary values. The Lab prefers centrally complementary for the latter.

Try it

Check a pair in the illustration: 10 − 2 = 8, and 10 − 8 = 2. Applying complement twice restores the values.

Relatedequivalencenormalmagic square
Symmetry / comparison

Equivalence

10

A declared relationship that treats two objects as the same for a particular comparison or count.

Before saying two squares are different, decide what transformations are allowed. A rotated square may be new to your notebook but not new to an enumeration.

More precisely

Two objects are equivalent under a declared set of transformations. For ordinary squares, the usual geometric transformations are the four rotations and four reflections, known as the dihedral group D4. The Lab records whether complements, relabelings, or higher-dimensional coordinate transformations are also allowed.

An orbit is the set of objects obtained from one object under the allowed transformations. A canonical representative is one selected member used for storage or counting.

Common confusion

“Unique” is incomplete unless the equivalence rules are stated.

Try it

Compare the four illustrated rotations. Their positions change; their entry set and magic sum do not.

Relatedcomplementline setnormal

These diagrams are original explanatory examples. Entries identify historical and source-dependent differences in terminology.

How the Lab checks things

Checks recompute sums from the displayed entries and test the entry range and repetition rules for that example. Each object states its required lines or groups. A lesson check marks the idea you demonstrated; it may be earned before the whole construction is finished.

Source images, transcriptions, teaching constructions, and transformed views have different origins. The linked source records explain which is being used. A valid array establishes an example, while a general construction claim needs a proof. Novelty and uniqueness require separate source and equivalence research.

Some historical terms have competing definitions, and some archive links are fragile. Those limitations remain with their records. The Lab does not treat a working link as proof that every claim in a source is correct.

The board textures and logo are AI-generated artwork. Historical source images retain their individual credits. Optimized display copies may omit embedded image credentials; original source assets are retained.
